title: Mountains: Geological Function in Scripture
subtitle: Examining scriptural imagery of mountains as Earth's stabilizers against modern geology
summary: The Quran presents mountains as firmly set features and signs of God's power. Geology shows that many mountains have deep roots and shape the crust locally, while tectonic mountain belts can also produce earthquakes. The verses are best read as truthful, accessible signs of an ordered earth—not as a claim that mountains prevent every earthquake.

seo.metaTitle: Mountains as Pegs in Scripture: Quran, Bible, and Geology
seo.metaDescription: Mountain imagery, geological evidence, and the Islamic call to reflect on creation without an earthquake-prevention slogan.

sections.title: What the Mountain Sign Asks Us to Notice
sections.body:
A mountain can be familiar and still be a sign: its scale, place in a landscape, and effects on the world around it challenge human self-importance. The Quran draws attention to such creation in a call to recognize God's power.

The claim should be read carefully. A mountain is not an earthquake-proof bolt holding every plate motion still. The Islamic invitation does not require that popular exaggeration, and an answer to criticism must not conceal what geology actually finds.

sections.title: Quranic Descriptions of Mountains
sections.body: The Quran calls mountains rawasi, firmly set features, and compares them to pegs (Quran 16:15; 21:31; 78:6–7). The verses connect mountains with habitability and God's order. They use common language, not geological terms.

sections.title: Biblical Language About Mountains
sections.body: The Bible also uses mountains poetically and theologically. They symbolize permanence, divine presence, and stability. Sinai, Zion, the Psalms, the Gospels, and Habakkuk use mountain imagery in varied ways. Like the Quran, these passages combine nature with theology.

sections.title: Why Earthquakes Are a Serious Test of the Claim
sections.body:
Mountain building can involve plate collision, volcanism, and crustal uplift. Many mountains have deep roots, but this does not make every range a fixed peg with the same geometry. Tectonically active mountain regions also experience earthquakes; the [USGS account of the 2025 Southern Tibetan Plateau earthquake](https://earthquake.usgs.gov/earthquakes/eventpage/us6000pi9w/executive) explains the collision and faulting context.

A claim that mountains universally prevent shaking would therefore be a poor description of the evidence. The proper response is to test that interpretation, not deny the observation.

sections.title: How the Image Should Be Understood
sections.body:
Quran 78:6-7 presents the earth as a resting place and mountains as pegs. Other stored passages speak of firmly set mountains. Muslim interpretation reads these images within the account of an ordered, habitable creation. They are not equations describing tectonic mechanisms.

The peg analogy can bring visible height and unseen depth to mind, but that is not proof that the verse uniquely predicted isostasy. A critic is entitled to question a more precise claim. The text, its context, and the scientific assertion must remain distinct.

Recognizing that distinction preserves a meaningful reading: the world provides conditions for life through an order people did not create. The argument then concerns its source and purpose, not the claim that every natural process is safe.

sections.title: Biblical Hermeneutics: Poetry, Prophecy, and Permanence
sections.body: Christian scholarship recognizes poetic and metaphorical mountain language. Psalms use hills as symbols. Jesus' power to move mountains is hyperbole. Habakkuk's crumbling mountains express creation's weakness before God. Such images teach transcendence and faith, not geology.

sections.title: Scholarly Approaches: Common Ground and Differing Emphases
sections.body:
Interpreters broadly treat mountain language as theological, not a technical account of tectonics. Some compare pegs with mountain roots as an analogy. The texts do not describe isostasy, and roots do not stop tectonic motion.

Geology does not confirm mountains as global stabilizers. Their theological meaning does not depend on that claim.

sections.title: A Sign Is More Than a Puzzle About Roots
sections.body:
The positive Islamic response is gratitude joined to responsibility. A landscape that supports life is not made morally irrelevant by understanding how it formed. Natural processes can be the means through which a Creator provides, rather than a rival to provision.

Someone unconvinced that there is a Creator needs that further argument. [Creation and Nature](/articles/creation-and-nature) develops it, including naturalistic alternatives. A mountain photograph alone is not enough to settle the question of God or the Quran's origin.

sections.title: Follow the Sign Without Exaggerating It
sections.body: The mountain passages invite reflection on creation and the limits of human power. They should not be reduced to an earthquake-prevention slogan. Continue with [How to Approach Scientific Claims](/articles/how-to-approach-scientific-claims-carefully) to test the argument fairly, and then consider the broader [case for the Quran](/articles/why-the-quran).

faq.question: Does the Quran claim that mountains are literally pegs that anchor Earth?
faq.answer: Quran 78:7 compares mountains to pegs, while verses such as 16:15 and 21:31 describe firmly set mountains in language of earthly stability. The image is truthful and accessible without being a technical model of plate tectonics. Many mountain ranges do have deep crustal roots, but the verses need not be made to claim that mountains physically anchor the whole planet or prevent earthquakes. Their larger purpose is to direct attention to God's ordering of a habitable world.

faq.question: Does modern geology confirm that mountains stabilize Earth?
faq.answer: Not in the popular sense that mountains stop the earth from shaking. Mountains commonly form through tectonic processes, and active mountain belts are often earthquake zones. Geology does show that many ranges have deep crustal roots and that mountains shape water, climate, erosion, and local crustal balance. These facts fit the Quran's observable imagery, but they should not be turned into a claim that geology has discovered global anti-earthquake pegs.

faq.question: How do Christian scholars interpret Biblical mountain passages?
faq.answer: Christian biblical scholarship recognizes that mountains in Scripture serve primarily theological and metaphorical purposes. Mountains symbolize permanence, divine presence, and God's authority. Biblical poetry (as in the Psalms) uses mountain imagery to inspire faith and worship. When Jesus speaks of 'moving mountains' through faith, this employs hyperbolic language common to both Hebrew and Greek rhetoric to emphasize the power of trust in God, not to make geological claims.

faq.question: Is there a conflict between Scripture's poetic language and scientific geology?
faq.answer: No fundamental conflict exists when Scripture's poetic purpose is understood. Neither the Quran nor the Bible was written to provide geological explanations. Both employ metaphorical language appropriate to their contexts and audiences to convey theological truths. Scientific investigation reveals the mechanisms; Scripture invites contemplation of divine design. A poem about the ocean as 'an infinite mirror' doesn't conflict with physics—it communicates truth through a different language and purpose.

faq.question: Why do both scriptures use mountain imagery if not to teach geology?
faq.answer: Mountains are prominent features in the natural world experienced by the audiences of these texts. They inspire awe, appear enduring and stable, and serve as boundaries and landmarks. Both the Quran and Bible employ mountains as theological signposts—inviting reflection on divine power, wisdom, and the stability of God's creation. Mountains make excellent vehicles for this spiritual message precisely because they are visibly impressive and seemingly permanent, qualities that serve as reminders of the transcendent.

faq.question: Do Muslim and Christian scholars disagree about the interpretation of these passages?
faq.answer: Within each tradition there is real diversity of opinion, both across history and today. Classical commentators in both traditions often treated mountains' stabilizing and enduring qualities as literal fact within pre-modern cosmologies, while many contemporary scholars—responding in part to modern scientific findings—favor reading these passages as poetic and metaphorical rather than as scientific claims. Both traditions have produced sophisticated interpretive frameworks that allow for scriptural reverence while also engaging scientific investigation. The genuine disagreement, when it occurs, is between literalist and metaphorical approaches, and which reading counts as 'mainstream' has shifted over time rather than being a settled, permanent matter.

furtherReading.title: Where the Conflict Really Lies: Science, Religion, and Naturalism
furtherReading.author: Alvin Plantinga
furtherReading.note: Philosophical analysis examining the relationship between scientific and scriptural language and worldviews, addressing whether apparent conflicts between science and scripture are genuine or stem from methodological confusion (Oxford University Press, 2011).

furtherReading.title: Approaching the Quran: The Early Revelations
furtherReading.author: Michael Sells
furtherReading.note: Literary and philological study of Quranic language and rhetoric, including analysis of how the Quran employs metaphor and poetic devices to communicate theological meaning to its original audience (White Cloud Press, 1999).

furtherReading.title: Plate Tectonics: An Insider's History of the Modern Theory of the Earth
furtherReading.author: Naomi Oreskes (ed.), with Homer Le Grand
furtherReading.note: Historical account of how plate tectonics theory developed and was confirmed, illuminating the actual mechanisms of mountain formation and crustal dynamics (Westview Press, 2001).

furtherReading.title: The Bible and the Believer: How to Read the Bible Critically and Religiously
furtherReading.author: Marc Zvi Brettler, Peter Enns, and Daniel J. Harrington
furtherReading.note: Three scholars—Jewish, evangelical Protestant, and Catholic—each explain how their own tradition reads Scripture in light of historical-critical scholarship, including how metaphorical and non-literal language is understood as authoritative within each community (Oxford University Press, 2012).
